newsitem.title: INDIA: FOCUS - IMF praises Indian reforms, seeks second wave.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - IMF praises Indian reforms, seeks second wave.

text.p: International Monetary Fund (IMF) managing director Michel Camdessus hailed India on Wednesday for completing a key round of economic reforms and asked New Delhi to go even further in order to join Asia's "tiger" economies.

Camdessus lauded path-breaking tax and import duty cuts proposed by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in his budget last week for the year starting in April, but cautioned against monetary and fiscal policies that could stoke inflation.
"The first wave of structural reforms was decisive, achieving results beyond initial expectations," Camdessus told a news conference on the last day of a four-day trip to India.
He said a slowdown in trade growth in the 1996/97 fiscal year signalled a small loss of the momentum of the free-market reforms launched in 1991.

"But at the same time, you have a distinct window of opportunity, to build on the achievements...to try to do the other half of the journey to catch up with the performance of the Asian tigers. And why not?"
Indian officials expect gross domestic product (GDP) to grow by 7.0 percent or more in 1997/98 and to close the current fiscal year with 6.8 percent growth.
Having cut tax rates and import duties, India must ease trade controls on consumer goods, push ahead with the privatisation of state companies and open up the banking and insurance sectors, he said.
India's export growth in the April-January 1996/97 period slipped to 6.19 percent from a heady peak of 22 percent in the same 10 months of the previous fiscal year.
"Most important and most urgent is the removal of quantitative restrictions on consumer goods," said Camdessus, who met Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and Chidambaram on Wednesday.

Camdessus urged India to funnel resources out of subsidies, defence spending and unproductive expenditure into infrastructure, particularly in the agriculture sector, and to free oil prices from subsidies and state controls.
The government owes state-run oil firms, which sell petroleum products on the domestic market at prices well below international levels, some 155 billion rupees ($4.3 billion).
In the federal budget announced last Friday, India slashed corporate and income taxes and targeted a fiscal deficit of 4.5 percent of GDP in 1997/98, compared with 5.0 percent in the current year.
Camdessus said a second round of fiscal consolidation must aim to cut state government deficits and also reduce the huge oil deficit arising from subsidised fuel.
He said a planned move to allow the convertibility of the rupee on the capital account would help India to integrate with the global economy.
At present, the rupee can be converted freely for trade in goods and services but the government controls capital transactions.

Asked whether he felt the government had risked a higher deficit by cutting taxes in its budget, Camdessus said: "When judged by past Indian and international experience, this is a bold and credible strategy."

But Camdessus said the government and the central bank must be vigilant to control inflation that might arise from a budgetary deficit resulting from a fall in anticipated revenue or a rise in expenditure.
Year-on-year inflation stood at 7.99 percent on February 15, compared with 4.60 percent a year earlier. ($ = 35.85 Indian Rupees)
